title: Downstream latency surge — SLO burn investigation (wip)
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from the on-call investigation into the SLO burn that started ~2025-11-02 22:10 UTC and peaked around 22:33 UTC. Primary symptom: large number of latency SLO alerts triggered for the hosted API model endpoint group (api-model-prod), followed by follow-on pager noise from error-rate alerts when retry logic kicked in.

Impact: 
- Affected: api-model-prod (tier-main) serving region us-west1. ~12% of requests breaching p50/p95 targets during the peak window.
- Customer-visible: intermittent slow generations (high tail latency), increased 5xx retries for some tenants using long-context routes.
- Duration: ~40m of elevated SLO burn; automatic fallbacks mitigated some traffic after 22:45.

Short timeline (observed):
- 22:08 UTC: first sparse latency alerts, noise increases quickly
- 22:10 UTC: SLO-burn alert aggregation threshold crossed (pager fired)
- 22:15 UTC: on-call triage — noticed elevated downstream Redis command latencies in dashboards
- 22:22 UTC: metric exporter for redis nodes restarted for one host (alerts about missing redis_exporter metrics appear)
- 22:30 UTC: retries from client layer cause 5xx surge and additional error-rate alerts
- 22:45 UTC: traffic shifted to fallback routing policy for tier-main; SLO burn begins to subside
- 23:00 UTC: metrics backfilled; some alert counts still catching up; incident closed to monitoring

Primary signals and dashboards examined:
- api_model_latency_p95 (per-route, per-model) — p95 spike correlated with queue depth 
- redis_cmd_duration_seconds_bucket (per-instance) — sustained high p99 on 22:10–22:25
- exporter_up{job="redis_exporter"} — show host exporter restarts around 22:22
- kube_pod_container_restart_count (redis-exporter pod) — restart recorded for redis-exporter-3
- request_queue_depth_gauge (serving runtime) — climbing concurrently with redis p99

Immediate hypotheses (ranked):
1) Downstream dependency (Redis) experienced transient latency increase due to CPU steal on the VM or garbage collector pause in a proxy process. This caused the inference runtime to block on KV lookups, increasing end-to-end latencies. Restart of redis_exporter is a secondary symptom (observability tooling restart), not the root cause.
2) Redis exporter restart caused temporary metric dropout which confused alerting aggregation and made the SLO-burn window appear worse; alert dedup/aggregation rules fired repeatedly as sensors flapped.
3) A sudden workload pattern (large batched prefix accesses from a single customer) amplified queued KV cache misses causing saturation and tail-latency increases.

Evidence/comments per hypothesis:
- Hypothesis 1: redis instance metrics (CPU, syscall wait) show small spike in system cpu and high rtt for a 2–3 minute window. Need to check host-level dmesg/syscalls.
- Hypothesis 2: exporter restart at 22:22 correlates with dropouts in redis_cmd_duration histogram (gap in data). But latency increase already started ~22:08, so exporter restart cannot fully explain the initial slope.
- Hypothesis 3: access heatmap from live traffic shows one client id with an unusually dense sampling pattern starting 22:06. Correlate with tenant logs.

Queries / checks to run (Prometheus / Logging):
- p95/p99 latency for api-model-prod route:
  sum by (route) (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(api_model_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)))
- redis p99 on host:
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redis_cmd_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, instance))
- exporter uptime: up{job="redis_exporter"} or kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{pod=~"redis-exporter-.*"}
- identify high-volume client ids: topk(10, sum(rate(api_model_requests_total[1m])) by (client_id))
- serving runtime queue depth vs inflight requests: max_over_time(request_queue_depth_gauge[10m]) and inflight_request_gauge

Immediate mitigations taken (during incident):
- Enabled fallback routing policy for tier-main to route 30% of traffic to smaller-capacity, lower-latency model variant to reduce pressure. (Action: Elena)
- Issued temporary rate-limit adjustments to aggressive retrying clients via API gateway (Action: Marcus)
- Increased Redis replicas for a subset of keys used by the hot-client flow (manual scale; Action: Samir)
- Restarted redis_exporter pod for host redis-3 to restore metrics; note: done late in window, may have caused momentary metric blips (Action: Priya)

What went wrong (observability + alerting design):
- Alert aggregation overly sensitive to short-term missing metric windows. When redis_exporter restarted, the metrics gap caused re-firing of threshold alerts instead of suppressing duplicates.
- No fast detection for hot-client behavior at the routing layer; we rely on aggregated per-route p95 but not per-client anomaly detection.
- Serving-runtime queue depth metric wasn't wired into the SLO-burn alerting rule as a suppressor; as a result, SLO alert fired without context to tell runbook to check downstream queueing.

Runbook DRAFT additions (short term):
1) Add a pre-flight triage checklist for SLO burn alerts: check downstream latency teachers (redis, db), check exporter_up signals, check queue depth, check top client ids.
2) Change alert aggregation: if exporter_up shows drop for >90s, suppress re-firing of the same downstream-latency alert for that host for 5m (avoid alert-churn).
3) Add a temporary play: automated fallback routing to alternate model variant when serving runtime queue depth > X for > 2m.
4) Add 'hot-client' breaker: quick throttle on top-k clients if they constitute > Y% of requests and correlate with p95 spike.

Longer-term mitigations and engineering work (owners):
- Observability: implement metric continuity checks and a short-lived buffer so that exporter restarts don't cause metric gaps to be treated as new incidents (Owner: Observability team - Marcus).
- Alerting: introduce cross-signal deduplication rules (slo-burn + exporter_up) and reduce noise by moving some alerts to a lower priority triage queue (Owner: SRE - Priya).
- Serving runtime: expose per-client heatmaps and make routing policy capable of per-client throttling and fast-fallback without manual intervention (Owner: Serving Runtime - Elena).
- Capacity planning: investigate redis sizing and hot-key sharding for KV cache patterns; consider memtier proxy to cushion backend latency (Owner: Platform Eng - Samir).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Why did exporter for redis-3 restart? Was it OOM/kube eviction/GC? Check kube event timeline and node syslogs (syscalls).
- Was there a deployment, config change, or noisy neighbor on the compute host around 22:00? Look at infra change window.
- Can we retroactively compute how many alerts were duplicate/noisy (i.e., would not have fired if exporter gaps were suppressed)?

Notes to self / on-call tips: 
- When SLO burn hits, quickly check exporter_up for key dependencies (redis, postgres, kube-state). A missing exporter often means metric flapping — treat that as an immediate suppressor in your head.
- If queue depth is rising but backend latencies look stable, consider hot-client behavior before scaling backends. Scaling can make hot-clients hide underlying cache-miss patterns.
- Remember rolling restarts of exporters are often done by automation; correlate with cluster-ops/cron.

Next immediate steps (owners / ETA):
- Priya: collect node syslogs + kube events for redis-3 (ETA: 2025-11-13)
- Marcus: prototype alert suppression rule in staging (ETA: 2025-11-17)
- Elena: design per-client heatmap dashboard and fast-throttle POC (ETA: 2025-11-24)
- Samir: run hot-key load tests against redis cluster and simulate fallback routing (ETA: 2025-11-20)

Appendix (commands / useful links):
- PromQL examples (copy to dashboard):
  topk(10, sum(rate(api_model_requests_total[1m])) by (client_id))
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redis_cmd_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, instance))
- Kibana queries: request_id: (search for client_id X) and logs between 2025-11-02T22:00:00Z and 2025-11-03T23:00:00Z
- Related tickets: JIRA-SRE-8791 (incident page), CONFLUENCE-DL-375 (post-incident writeup link)

(End of scratchpad — convert to formal postmortem if follow-up confirms root cause.)
